title: Kernel compatibility scorecard + online tuner for arch/seq-len-aware selection
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
We currently rely on coarse heuristics to pick kernels for attention and matmul paths. This leads to suboptimal tail latency and avoidable token cost when serving mixed workloads (short chat turns, long prefill batches, and heterogeneous GPU types).

Goal:
Create a friction-light compatibility scorecard that quantifies kernel performance vs model architecture, sequence-length bucket, batch shape, KV-cache usage, and GPU topology. Use that scorecard as the input to an online tuner that can safely switch kernels at runtime with rollback on regressions. The scoreboard should drive both prefill and decode scheduling decisions.

Success criteria / Acceptance:
- Compatibility scorecard produced for every kernel variant in the catalog (float score for latency, memory headroom, and cost per token) across seqlen buckets: 0-64,65-256,257-1024,1025+.
- Online tuner prototype that can: 1) run lightweight microprobes on idle cycles, 2) recommend a preferred kernel per route within 5 minutes of traffic pattern change, 3) execute a canary switch and measure tail latency and error rates, and 4) rollback on >5% tail-latency regression or functional failures.
- Integration into request router so prefill requests prefer kernels with better memory headroom and decode requests prefer lower token-latency kernels.
- End-to-end dashboard showing comparison between baseline heuristic and scorecard-driven selection (latency P50/P95/P99, cost delta, fallback count).

Design notes and tradeoffs considered:
- Scorecard vs full cost model: scorecard is a simpler empirical surface that we can compute per-kernel quicker than deriving an analytic cost model. It will capture micro-architectural quirks (tensor core behavior, occupancy cliffs).
- Probing frequency: aggressive probing gives faster adaptation but risks extra noise and overhead. We prefer low-rate microprobes (0.1-0.5% of traffic) and synthetic probes during idle windows.
- Switching safety: we adopt staged canaries (single-request probe -> 1% traffic -> 10% traffic) with continuous metrics-driven gates. This reduces blast radius compared to immediate route-wide swaps.
- Prefill vs decode asymmetry: prefill workloads benefit from memory-headroom-oriented kernels (higher throughput, better batch packing). Decode workloads prioritize low incremental token-latency. Scorecard exposes both axes and the router weights them by request type.

Plan / Milestones:
1) Scorecard schema and microbenchmark harness (2 weeks) — define metrics (latency median/tail, memory margin, per-token cost), implement harness that can run on multiple GPU types and record to perf store.
2) Populate initial scorecard for 6 top kernels across 3 GPU types and 3 models (2 weeks).
3) Online tuner prototype with safe canary rollout and rollback (3 weeks).
4) Router integration and prefill/decode weighting policy (1 week).
5) Dashboard and experiment run comparing baseline -> scorecard tuner (1 week).

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/120550/Kernel+Compatibility+Scorecard+Design
- Microbenchmark harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/feature/scorecard-harness
- Early PR for harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2045
- Canary runtime hooks PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2061
- Benchmark dashboard (Grafana): https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/scorecard/scorecard-comparison

Outstanding decisions / open questions:
- Should the scorecard be stored centrally (global) or sharded per-region? Central gives faster global learnings but may miss region-specific hardware mixes. Proposal: global canonical scorecard with region-specific adjustments (multiplier factors) recorded from local probes.
- How to credit KV-cache interactions that are stateful across requests? We will capture "effective headroom" for prefill pathways by measuring end-to-end batch build times with KV enabled vs cold KV.
- Bandit vs deterministic tuner: initial implementation will be deterministic (rules + thresholds) to simplify safety and observability. We can iterate to a Bayesian bandit later.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: microprobes could perturb production latency. Mitigation: run probes at <0.5% traffic and prefer synthetic probes during low-util windows.
- Risk: dataset drift (model or tokenizer changes) could invalidate scorecard. Mitigation: schedule re-profiling weekly and version the scorecard with model fingerprints.
- Risk: GPU scheduler interactions (MIG, multi-tenancy) change effective performance. Mitigation: record occupancy and tenant signals as part of probe metadata; downgrade confidence when noisy.

Delivery checklist (owner: Miguel Hernandez):
- [ ] Scorecard schema checked in and documented (Confluence + README)
- [ ] Harness runs across target GPUs and produces baseline CSVs
- [ ] Tune engine can perform staged canaries and rollbacks automatically
- [ ] Router honors scorecard weights for prefill/decode paths
- [ ] Dashboard compares baseline heuristic vs scorecard-driven selection
- [ ] Runbook for debugging kernel regressions and rollbacks
